title: DiScammer Defender local completion record
body_md:
## A local record of practice

The checkpoints below are based on lesson marks and the self-assessment result stored in this browser. To create a personal completion record, all lessons in all nine modules must be marked complete here, and the final self-assessment must have a saved result of **80% or higher**. Enter the name you want printed on the record. The record is generated in this browser. DiScammer does not issue, sign, proctor or validate it. If you explicitly enable optional progress sync, an encrypted progress bundle can include the exam result and name; the server receives ciphertext, not a readable record. Clearing browser storage can remove the local copy, and another device will not show it unless you import or sync progress. If helpful, use **Print / Save as PDF** for a personal copy.

This record is **not a credential, identity document, independently verified score or evidence that you can prevent a real scam**. A high score is a prompt to practise, not permission to skip verification. An old passing result may persist after a lower retake, so reflect on the questions you just missed even if the checkpoint stays green.

## Make a personal safety plan — keep it private

Spend five minutes writing a plan somewhere you control, such as a private note or paper. Do not type account numbers, passwords, codes, real incident narratives or financial details into this lesson.

1. **Pause trigger.** Write one sentence you will use when a message asks for a sudden payment, secret, login or change of account: “I will check this through a route I choose.” Give yourself permission to interrupt urgency.
2. **Independent contacts.** Save the real bank support route from your card or banking app, one family contact, and the workplace contact for payment or security questions. Record where to find them, not secret access details. Recheck them when they change.
3. **Account basics.** Pick your primary email and banking accounts. Check for unique passwords or available passkeys, supported MFA, current recovery contacts and safe backup methods. A passkey improves a supported sign-in path but does not fix a weak recovery route.
4. **Payment rule.** For a new payee, changed bank account or exceptional transfer, pause and confirm the exact recipient and purpose with a known contact. Use a second approver if your organization requires one. A real request can wait for the control.
5. **If something happened.** Note what was exposed—money, a password, a code, device access or identity data. Contact the relevant provider through its official route promptly; request the remedy appropriate to the payment method; secure the affected account; keep dates and references. Recovery is not guaranteed, and reporting routes vary by country.
6. **Practice with someone.** Tell one trusted person your callback rule without sharing private details. Agree on a calm way to verify a surprising request, including when a voice or video seems familiar. A code word may help but should not be the only check.

### Reflection before you print

Which two exam or simulation decisions did you find hardest, and which independent route would you use in a real version of each? What would change if the request were legitimate? If you cannot answer yet, revisit those lessons and update the plan. The useful outcome is a habit you can carry beyond this browser, not the appearance of the record.

**Sources and scope.** This plan adapts UK NCSC [scam verification](https://www.ncsc.gov.uk/collection/phishing-scams/spot-scams) and [account recovery](https://www.ncsc.gov.uk/guidance/recovering-a-hacked-account), NIST [authenticator distinctions](https://pages.nist.gov/800-63-4/sp800-63b/authenticators/), and US FTC [payment-response advice](https://consumer.ftc.gov/articles/what-do-if-you-were-scammed), all checked 2026-10-20. They support habits, not a DiScammer qualification. Your bank, service, employer and local law determine actual steps.
